We are very happy to have that statement from the minister, and within a few days we shall expect a statement as to just what the government intends to do to meet the unemployment situation. Regardless of what the minister has just said1, the impression has gone abroad and has been created by government speakers that this amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act is being made for the purpose of meeting the present unemployment situation. It has been accepted as the government's proposal to meet the problem.
I certainly want to emphasize again-and this has already been done-that an increase in unemployment insurance is no substitute for work. If it is the government's policy for meeting unemployment then it is a complete reversal of their policy for the post-war years. From finance minister after finance minister we have heard year after year that the government's policy to meet unemployment was

Unemployment Insurance to provide a shelf of public works which could be put into operation whenever unemployment became serious. I submit that the time has come for the implementation of that policy. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), speaking particularly of the construction industry, was quoted in one of the Toronto daily papers on February 17 as follows:
Activity in the construction industry is still as buoyant as it has been since the end of the war, but it may be that we will shortly be moving into a new phase in which demand will not be quite so insistent.
That may not be altogether a bad thing. I am sure that many of you must have felt in recent years that a period of consolidation would have to come; that the spiral of increasing costs could not continue; and that, in the long run, everyone in the community, including your own industry, would benefit by the return of some pressure for higher productivity and somewhat lower production costs.
I take this statement to mean that it is the accepted policy of the government to invite such a period of unemployment as we have at the present time in order to provide a surplus of workers, so that costs of production may be reduced and productivity increased.
I think we should accept as a fact that the unemployment situation as it exists in Canada today is the responsibility of the federal government. In 1945 and 1949 the Liberal party took credit for the number of jobs that were available and for the general prosperity of the country. That, they told us from billboards and in other advertising, was the result of the policies of the Liberal government. By the same token, if they are going to take credit for the prosperity that existed during those years, they must take responsibility for the lack of jobs that is developing today. Whether or not the federal government should assume the financial responsibility in connection with providing jobs, certainly it is up to the federal government to take the initiative in bringing together governments at various levels so that when unemployment does strike us, as it is striking us today, public works programs will be available. Today we are actually back where we were before the war, as far as the unemployment situation is concerned. The federal government is passing the buck to the provincial governments; the provincial governments are passing it to the municipalities. The municipalities are coming back to the provincial governments and the federal government, and there has been practically no improvement in the last ten years, though it was realized that some steps should be taken to co-ordinate the efforts of governments at the three levels in order to meet this situation. Not until this fall are we to have a dominion-provincial conference to deal with responsibility of governments at various levels in regard to such social measures. For years opposition groups and

others have been clamouring for the government to bring together provincial and municipal authorities and take the initiative in bringing about some agreement so that when such situations develop we may be prepared for them.
Reference has been made to the fact that unemployment insurance, even as it may be improved by these amendments, will still provide less than the amount of relief paid in some of our municipalities. Unemployment insurance was never intended to take the place of employment. It was never intended to do more than tide a worker over the period of transition between losing one job and finding another; and we should never come to look upon unemployment insurance as a substitute for employment itself. From what I can gather the average married man receiving unemployment insurance gets something like $16 a week. In the case of a man with three or four children $16 a week, even if he were getting it for a period of time, would not be sufficient to maintain his family. In York township we pay in relief to a family of three $60.88 a month, plus rent; to a family of four, $84 a month plus rent; to a family of five, $92 a month, plus rent; and to a family of seven $125, plus rent. Unemployment insurance does not begin to maintain a family with five or six children, and can in no circumstances be expected to take the place of a weekly pay cheque.
Now there are one or two questions I want to ask the minister before I conclude. Within the last hour I have been informed by a member of the unemployment advisory committee that the amendments brought in this afternoon have not come before that committee, and that they have not been before the representatives of employees and employers who form that advisory committee.

I should like to ask the minister to give a little further explanation about the effect of these amendments. In order to put the question, I must refer to the situation in my own city of Vancouver. We have had extensive unemployment there; it has been as bad there perhaps as anywhere in Canada in recent weeks. As I understood the minister this afternoon, the only groups who would be helped by these amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act are those whose benefits have been exhausted or those who would be eligible for unemployment insurance if they had made further contributions. Then there is to be provision for two new groups who have not been making contributions; and as I understood1 it, they are groups which will be brought under the act eventually. But is any provision whatever being made for those people who do not come under any one of the four groups?
For example, although I do not know how many are involved, quite a few of the men who are unemployed in Vancouver this winter would not be in any of these four categories. A great many of them are younger men, and in many cases I think they have drifted to the coast with the belief that we always have a mild winter there. No doubt a good many of them came there with that belief in mind, but I am afraid they have been sadly disillusioned this winter. The situation, however, is tragic. These young men cannot be cared for either by the province or by the city, because they are employable. The city and the province will care only for those people who are not able to work. The result is that there is this large group who can get food only by going to the Salvation Army or to one or other of the churches. These agencies have done excellent work during the winter weeks, but that situation simply cannot go on. These men are considered, by the provincial authorities and by the municipal authorities, to be the sole responsibility of the dominion. Rightly or wrongly, that is the belief; and action is based on that belief. There is a good reason too for that belief, because the dominion, in making its proposals in 1945, said that it would undertake the responsibility for all the employables in Canada.
Will the minister tell the committee just what can be done for these men? Their plight is tragic. There is a gap there which must be filled, and I believe it must be filled by the dominion government. It is unfortunate that action has not already been taken to do something about that particular group. Will

My hon. friend has raised a larger question that is not envisaged by the amendments or by the Unemployment Insurance Act. We must keep before us what we are seeking to do in this measure, although we may have our views about its adequacy or inadequacy. What we are dealing with here now are amendments to the existing Unemployment Insurance Act which provide for supplementary benefit payments in the case of four different classes of workers. Admittedly these amendments will not cover all the workers, but they will cover those who come within the ambit of the four classes I have mentioned.
With regard to the question as to the responsibility for unemployed employables, that is not germane to this particular bill. I do not wish by any means to depreciate the importance of that matter, but this is not the place to discuss it; we would be out of order. Admittedly it is a problem that exists, but we can deal now only with the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
As I pointed out in my statement this afternoon, what we have done is this. We have observed the principles underlying the Unemployment Insurance Act itself, we have recognized the actuarial basis of that act, we have recognized the insurance aspects of that act, and have provided supplemental payments for those who come within its ambit during a certain period. First there are the individuals who have exhausted their benefits after March 31. Second, those who have not made the required 180 contributions but who made 90 contributions within the period after March 31 before the moment of claim. Such people will be covered as well as those who, if they have not made any contributions, have worked for a period of 90 days within the last twelve months of an eighteen-month period in lumbering and logging. And then another group who work in newly insured industries for 90 days. The amendment is to cover those. We are seeking to deal with those four classes; and the extent to which we deal with those four classes is a matter that alone is germane to the discussion at the moment, in my opinion, without in any way failing to appreciate the quality and the character of the general problem which does not come within the ambit of this measure.

I feel that hon. members in this house ought to be acquainted with the situation that developed on the Pacific coast. Hon. members of all parties from the greater riding areas of Vancouver, together with the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, took it upon themselves, at the invitation of the city council and also a general invitation of the trades and labour council and the Canadian Legion in that area, to do what we felt would be a benefit in an endeavour to solve this emergency of unemployment, which we had on the Pacific coast this year to an unprecedented extent, of some 12-9 per cent. All of these hon. members whom I have mentioned attended all or some of these meetings. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, I think, as well as myself, had the honour of attending all of these meetings.
I am perfectly content with this legislation as it has been presented, because in large measure, perhaps to the extent of 90 per cent, it embraces the needs and requirements of the spokesmen of labour at these various meetings we attended in the labour temple in Vancouver during the months of December and January last.
The bringing in of these additional groups is, in my opinion, a farsighted and humanitarian legislative enactment by the government, and for that I give them full marks, despite any derogatory remarks that may be made to the contrary before this legislation receives its final readings. But in that regard no one can possibly conceive of the Unemployment Insurance Act as a complete payment over a long-extended period in lieu of employment. It was never so intended, and I do not believe any government in Canada will at any time endeavour to make it of that type; but it does cover the emergency conditions which come to the various parts of Canada at different times. It is also now embracing a large field that was not subject to benefits and which, in my opinion, it was justifiably entitled to. This legislation brings it to a consummation.
I cannot look upon this legislation as other than a great step forward. This afternoon reference was made to the fact that we are

not developing employment by amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is quite true. But, in heaven's name, we are dealing with the Unemployment Insurance Act, and the amendments are not measures designed to bring about continuous and full employment for all.
A question was raised this afternoon by hon. members who I am quite sure are better acquainted with the legislative program contained in this legislation than I am, because they have been here longer than I have been. When they said that this legislation does not create jobs, I agreed with them. Certainly, it does not create jobs, and it never was intended to create jobs. It is a cushion and a barrier against continuing unemployment caused through emergencies or seasonal operations, and nothing more.
We ought to stick to the principles of the legislation rather than run foul of it, in connection with suggestions about creation of jobs. If we stick to the principles of the Unemployment Insurance Act I believe that we will all be able to go back to our constituencies-I for one will be, and I am quite sure this will apply to all the Vancouver members-and be proud of the legislation that is proposed in these amendments.
In my riding of Vancouver-Burrard there are possibly as great a number of those who will benefit from the bill, and who had previously been excluded from benefiting under the act, as there are in any riding in British Columbia. I shall be proud to go back to that riding of workmen, men and women who are, I am quite sure, going to be extremely satisfied with the amendments introduced to the Unemployment Insurance Act by the acting minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

There are one or two questions I want to ask, but before I ask them I should like to make this comment. During the discussion today we have made criticisms of the bill from this side of the house as to its inadequacy, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the minister and others, have replied that this measure is not the answer to the unemployment problem, that it is just a case of further tailoring of the Unemployment Insurance Act. May I remind the minister, and those who have said this sort of thing, that the only reference in the program of the government for this session- in other words, in the speech from the throne -to anything it proposes to do about unemployment is to the effect that changes are to be made with respect to unemployment insurance. These members have said that this is not the solution to the unemployment problem, and in that respect they agree with us.


Well then, what is the government's solution? When do we get some answer to this pressing problem? If we are not getting that, surely we are only doing our duty to point out the gross inadequacies of this measure in terms of the small amounts workers are to receive, the small number who will receive them, and the limited! period of time for which they will receive these benefits.
The question I want to put to the minister was put to him perhaps more than once during the discussion this afternoon. Did the unemployment insurance advisory committee have a chance to consider these proposals? I mean the major ones, the ones having to do with these four new classes, the fact that there is to be only an 80 per cent benefit for a certain number of days, and so on. Did the committee have these proposals before them and did they concur in the proposals that are now in this measure?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

They are an important body when you have some hot potato you want to get rid of, but now wheni the government has a proposal to bring in that is inadequate it is pretty obvious they were -not consulted at all.

Then there is another group who have worked ninety days within the last twelve months of the eighteen-month period, and then there is the group who have worked ninety days in a group just recently made insurable. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister about the case of a young man, for instance, who is employed in the fishing industry for ninety days. When the bill is considered it would seem to me that these are points as to which we could very well have new amendments. We are trying to suggest to the minister now some of the weaknesses of the act. I think matters of that sort should be taken under consideration because the present measure is going to be of very little benefit, so far as I can see, in helping the unemployment situation in the province of New Brunswick. I know it is not in the act, but it seems to me when we bring in a bill of this kind to assist men who are out of employment we should prepare a bill which will be of benefit to the men who really need it. That is the point I wish to make.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I want to ask the minister one or two questions about the advisory committee, but before I do so I wish to say a word about the insurance feature of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think if we insist upon saying that everyone who contributes towards the fund must get something out of it, we are just being unrealistic. This is insurance against unemployment. If a person contributes to the act for thirty years and does not have to call upon the fund for benefits, it seems to me that it is his good fortune. It is a social arrangement where the fortunate person who continues in employment helps out the person who is not so fortunate. So much for that part of it.
We should always try to make sure that, when a person has paid into the unemployment insurance fund and then leaves that employment and goes into uninsurable employment, without a period of unemployment, then the insurance fund he has accumulated during the time he was contributing should not be lost to him. He should be able to take advantage of it at some other time. I do not know to what extent the contributor is protected against such an eventuality. I think we should see that he is protected so far as possible.
I should like to ask a question about the advisory committee. Who are the members of the advisory committee? What interests will the two new members represent? I understand that the members on the advisory committee represent either employer or employee interests, and I was wondering whether the minister could give that information. Is the advisory committee not important enough to refer amendments of this kind to it for its decision? If it is not that important, why should the advisory committee be enlarged?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks a perfectly reasonable question. The purpose of the enlargement, I may say offhand, is to take in representatives of the railroad brotherhoods. At the moment, I cannot give the personnel of the committee. I could give the name of Mr. George Burt, and I know Mr. Mackintosh is the chairman. There are several others, and I have sent for a list of the names.
The advisory committee is a body which seeks to advise the commission in respect of the act. It is exactly what its name implies. It deals largely with the ways and means of improving the existing provisions of the act. For instance, it deals with such questions as the waiting day period. Quite a number of the amendments that are going to be introduced are amendments to the existing act which have been considered by the existing advisory committee and, in most instances, unanimously approved.

Unemployment Insurance
The supplementary benefit is an entirely new procedure. It is not something that arises out of the existing act, but is something that is supplementary to it. It is the sort of matter for which the government, after consideration by an interdepartmental committee-at which time the commission had an opportunity of making its point of view known-has to accept the responsibility, which responsibility the government is accepting.

I should like to ask the minister a question about the contributions which are now being increased for certain insured classes. During the time the Unemployment Insurance Act was being considered in committee, a good deal of stress was laid on the actuarial position of the unemployment insurance fund. As the minister will perhaps recall, there were a number of alternate proposals which the government declined to accept, because they were trying to put the fund on what was known as a proper actuarial foundation. I am only speaking from memory now, but I think my memory is fairly clear, when I say that was one of the reasons advanced at one sitting for not including certain special groups in the original plan. It was felt it would disturb the actuarial soundness of the fund.
I take it that now the government has stepped into the picture it has, in some way, destroyed the actuarial position in which the fund was. When I say that, I am not suggesting I am opposed to it, because at this time I think that is essential. I do believe, however, if we are going to disturb the actuarial basis-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: There is not going to be any disturbance whatsoever of this fund. The supplementary benefit payments will be taken care of in the way I have indicated, by premiums imposed on the employee and the employer, and the difference will be provided for out of the consolidated fund. The insurance fund now amounts to $589,642,210.67, and will not in any way be depreciated.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I do not think the minister understands my point. Perhaps I did not state it clearly. It seems to me the very fact that the government has now decided to guarantee the fund indicates that the actuarial position will be changed. One thing that disturbed me particularly about the bill, as described by the minister in the resolution stage, was that the workers are now going to have to pay one cent a day more than they were paying before; that would apply to industry as well. If the unemployment situation increases as it has, and becomes general, I am wondering whether or not the government is fair in asking the worker to put up


that extra money to cover a nation-wide condition, instead of having the government take care of that by guaranteeing the fund. If the actuarial position is being disturbed, then it seems to me that the government is going a long way in asking the workingmen of Canada to put up another cent to cover a condition for which I think this federal government has some responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

I can only repeat, because it is important that I should repeat, that the actuarial soundness of the fund, in the opinion of those who are by training and experience qualified to judge

I mention no less a person than Mr. Watson, the actuary, and others- is not being disturbed in any way.
In regard to the other question raised by the hon. member about imposing a cent a day on the worker and employer, all we are doing is simply maintaining the insurance principle. Upon reflection, I think the hon. member will agree that is the thing to do.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the minister, but it is one that has already been asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I just wanted to make an observation with regard to the actuarial position which has just been mentioned. I think the minister will agree with me that it is not precisely the same as it was when this plan was inaugurated. In other words, what I am trying to say is this. The moneys that your employees put into that fund find their way into the consolidated revenue fund. The Minister of National Revenue shakes his head, saying no. I hope he is right. Even if it does, it would be on a sound basis. I should like to see tabled in this house a statement showing where this $589,642,210.67 actually is, not that I am afraid that it will not be immediately available when it is called on, but if the record is checked carefully-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I think it is in the public accounts.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BENEFITS DURING WINTER SEASON-VARIOUS AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Yes, it is in the public accounts; that is quite true. Our good triend, Mr. Graham Towers, whom I should like to call as a witness, made sure it went into the public accounts. But the public accounts, when they are all added together, show overwhelming surpluses. Let us remember that $589,630,000 of this money does not belong to the government of Canada. Let us be ordinary practical bookkeepers. It belongs not to the government of Canada but to our employees. Some day, and I hope it is not too soon, it will have to be paid back to those of us who have served industry and what not. Perhaps that day may not be too far distant. It will be paid back rapidly, and when the public accounts are dissipated to the extent of half a billion dollars or more we and the people of Canada, on looking at the financial statement of Canada's affairs, will not be quite as happy as we are today, with revenues which are so high. I do not mention this matter particularly to be critical. I mention it merely that we might be sensible about the position in which we find ourselves. I do not want in any way to detract from the necessity of unemployment insurance; but our bookkeeping system should be of a kind that would show the exact position, so that we would not be carried away by the almost overwhelming, I would say, superfluity of funds, some of which, to the extent of $589 million, is not our money. It belongs to those of our employees who each week have had so much deducted from them. I think the minister could explain to the house that with the advent of Graham Towers our bookkeeping system was changed just a little bit. A great number of members of this chamber have a wrong idea with regard to the surpluses that we, on the whole, have in Canada. We have a bad habit of carrying into those surpluses some of the moneys that belong to some of our employees, in the same way as many men perhaps carry some of the money which belongs to their wives in their own account. I think we should tell the public the position and be quite frank about it. I think we should tell them that that is not our money, but that it belongs to those who have served industry and otherwise since the advent of the Unemployment Insurance Act.

Mr. Speaker, may I join those who have spoken in this debate in congratulation of the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address. In addition I venture to congratulate the leaders of the various parties in this house upon the excellent speeches which they have made on this occasion. I was particularly pleased that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) spent a good portion of the time allotted to him in advocating federal aid for education, a cause to which I have myself in the past given some time and effort, and one which I hope to promote further in the future. But it is not with that subject that I wish to deal tonight.
The speech from the throne was just what one would have expected. Its failings have been advanced by various opposition speakers who have preceded me. To me it was a vague admission that the state of things in the nation was not quite as it should be, and the pious hope that the deterioration would not continue. Apparently we must wait and see. We are, forsooth, not the masters of our own destiny, but rather its victims. There is little sign of action on the part of the government to guide it.


I hope to say a word or two on foreign affairs. After the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), one feels somewhat diffident in approaching that subject; but my courage is bolstered by the fact that, as I have been thinking, it is no mean thing to be a free member of a free parliament possessing a right equal to that given to all others, to express freely one's own ideas in this House of Commons, whether those ideas may be considered right or wrong.
It has often occurred to me that a very small proportion of the members in this house do discuss foreign affairs, or in fact many matters outside our own boundaries, even when these matters pertain to our own affairs and have a direct bearing upon them. The average member appears to shun such debates. I have sought in my own mind for a reason for that. Is it perhaps a relic of the long period in which our international diplomacy was handled almost entirely by the mother country, Great Britain? Can it be that, awed by the wealth and power of our immediate neighbour, we are diffident about advancing independent views on international matters, letting the United States speak to some extent for us? Is it perhaps an insularity produced by our geographical position and the fact of our remoteness from the ferment of Europe and of Asia and of being surrounded, as we are, by two great oceans? Well, sir, insularity in these days is a difficult position to maintain. The impact of world affairs must be felt even by those who would avoid them or who have no interest in them. World problems have become our problems.
I have said that there is little discussion of international affairs in this house. Such debate as there is is largely in the form of pronouncements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We listen with an awe invoked perhaps by envy, or perhaps to some degree by the recognition of his greater opportunities to obtain information upon those particular subjects. But let me say, sir, that we must not, with all due respect to the minister, leave the evolution of Canada's foreign policy to the mind of one man, however brilliant that mind or that man may be.
The recent speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was to me a disappointment. I have no doubt that it was a disappointment too to the diplomats who crowded into the galleries to hear him. It was a delightful and interesting travelogue by a genial globe traveller. It might just as well

have been given by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), who shared the minister's journeyings.
A moment ago I spoke of the minister's speeches as pronouncements. Well, in this speech there was certainly no pronouncement, no announcement of a firm decision, no statements of government policies. Are these decisions, if any have been made, to be clothed in that same cloak of secrecy in which the government has been so successful in wrapping certain other matters? Or could it be that this Canada has perhaps no independent foreign policy and must wait until that policy is formulated for her by other governments? We would have liked to hear what decision has been made in regard to the recognition or the non-recognition of China, upon which an early statement had been promised. We would have liked to be given a gleam of hope for betterment in what we call the cold war situation, and to have been told that some action had been taken by the government upon which such a hope could have been based.
Throughout the speech there was one welcome note. The minister said that he and the government realized the need for supporting with sympathy and with material aid1 the new nations of the East to the end that they may preserve their independence and their freedom, and here I might suggest investment of sterling which we can obtain for our surplus products and which we could invest in those countries. But again apparently no firm decisions have been made or at least announced as to the amount of our commitment in that direction.
The minister made the point that our commitments in the East would necessarily be limited by the fact of our commitment in the Atlantic sphere. In the light of the minister's statement that the centre of gravity of world affairs has moved now to eastern Asia, one might ask if there had been any review of commitments in the western sphere. We should like to have heard how successful in that sphere we have been in promoting the objects for which those commitments were given.
There are feelings of unease in the country in regard to that. The government's opinion, and the opinion I think of the great majority of Canadians, is that those commitments were necessary as a security measure against possible aggression, and as an active step towards promotion of economic co-operation and world peace. There is a small body of opinion -and I am glad that it is small-which would oppose any co-operation, through their desire to aid a foreign power. Their numbers, as I have said, are fortunately few. Then there
The Address-Mr. Knight is a third and honest and loyal group of thinking people who are worried lest our commitments may involve us, not in co-operation and in human understanding, but in a struggle not necessarily based upon ideologies, but upon the rivalry of two powerful nationalistic and sovereign states. We would have liked some reassurances which might have been for us a renewal of our faith. So much for the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The speech from the throne too was disappointing, in that it lacked any constructive proposal for the improvement of what we call loosely the international situation. An absence of expressed optimism is easy to understand. For indeed the situation there does continue, if one may accept the opinion of the press, to deteriorate. We as a nation seem to have no solution, and we are pinning a shaky faith to an increased and crippling program of defence.
The minds of the peoples of the world, sir, are possessed with deadly fear, the fear of war. This fear is shared equally by the people of my constituency and of my province. The people of England are thinking about the same thing. Mr. Churchill knew that very well when he introduced into one of his election speeches the other day a promise that if he were elected he would try to do something about bringing about a cessation of these war preparations which presage disaster. He would have been the last man to have suggested discussions with the Soviet union at the highest level, unless he had known that there was in the hearts of the people a response to that desire and that call for peace. The people of England have much to fear from another war. They know that in such an event their little island will simply be an advance air station, an advance depot and air base for one of the two mighty antagonists; and as such they can be only a target of the life-destroying missiles of the other.
Dare one in these times, in this nation and in this assembly, lift up his voice in the cause of peace, without having his motives misunderstood? Dare one suggest the truism that war settles nothing permanently? Dare one warn this house that, with the atomic bomb and the hydrogen bomb extant, war would be the ultimate disaster? Dare one say that it would promote the spread of the very scourge which we now by our every effort oppose? To me it is an awful thing that men can even contemplate the use of the destructive weapons which they have under their hand. We are not in these days training great armies of fighting men. They have become obsolete. War has been robbed of any of the manly attributes that it might ever have had.

The Address-Mr. Knight No, we do not train infantry soldiers any more; we put our faith in scientists and technicians. And by that very fact we are admitting that war in the future is to lose those manly attributes, if it ever could be said to have had any, and become a conflict as to which side can destroy first and most completely the civilian populations of unarmed men, women and little children.
Sir, these are gruesome things to contemplate, but I think once in a while the truth about them should be said. I have pictured to the house Hiroshima to the nth degree. The survivors will be the winners and there might not be too many of them to get ready for the next contest.
Someone, I have forgotten who, upoh being asked what would be the weapons in the ;hird world war, said that he did not know what the weapons of the third world war would be, but he did think that the weapons of the fourth world war would likely be bows and arrow*.
Somehow or other the people of the world will have to get together and solve this problem. Somehow or other mutual distrust and misunderstanding, among peoples and among nations, will have to be dispelled. I am familiar, as we all are, with the attempts which we have made in that direction. I make no excuse for any government that has been the means of blocking those attempts, nations that indeed have shut off their populations from intercourse with the rest of the peoples of the world.
I, myself, believe in freedom of communication, freedom of discussion, freedom to choose for ourselves any form of government that we wish. In short, I believe in democracy-political, social and economic. But my whole life-and this has been the experience of most hon. members in the house-has consisted of two great cycles, each composed of three parts. Each of those parts has been induced by the one which has preceded it. They are all interdependent, one upon the other. Two great cycles, I say, or a series of the three states-depression, war and prosperity. And each of them is the cause of the one which follows upon it.
At what stage of that cycle do we now find ourselves? Well, hon. members will have to decide that for themselves. But the year 1912 and the year 1929 keep intruding themselves upon my own thinking as corresponding to the present time. We must somehow or other learn to break that cycle. It would be a disastrous thing if people were to accept such a cycle as necessary and inevitable. And it would be a greater tragedy if our young people were to accept war as a necessary prelude to the good life, to the extent that

when faced with a state of depression they might become reconciled to accepting, in the course of things, war as an alternative.
The problem of peace, at the moment apparently insoluble, must be solved. I know not what such a solution may involve. It may involve some sacrifice of national sovereignty. It may ultimately involve some form of world government. We have been called upon many times and oft to make sacrifices in the cause of war. Someone, somewhere, somehow- probably some nation-may be called upon to make sacrifices in the cause of peace. And when I speak of peace I do not do so in any sentimental or emotional way. I do not mean peace at any price. I am well aware that a state of peace can be a state of uneasy mistrust and suspicion.
The peace which I hope for must be based upon law and order, and that will have to be on an international level. I should like to ask Canada to take some initiative in the pursuit of a peace of that kind.
There are many people in this country who think that the diplomacy of our own Department of External Affairs is guided by the corresponding government department in the United States. The fact that we are allied with the United States for purposes of defence certainly does not, nor should it, imply that we should follow the lead of that nation in all matters, nor that we should imitate it slavishly in its decisions upon international relations. Personally I have no wish that Canada should become, either in peace or in war, the tail of the American comet. Perhaps it may sound ridiculous that I, in my humble place, should'pass judgment upon a nation of 180 million people; but I venture the suggestion that the United States has given evidence of some naivete in its foreign policy which has not been evident in the foreign policy of other nations-and I am thinking notably of Great Britain. I am thinking of how Great Britain handled the problem of India, bowing to the inevitable, and at the right time and, may I say, under circumstances which left little if any of the old bitterness as between what had been master country and colony, but rather left a feeling of friendship and co-operation for the years to come.
I am considering, and I am sure the Asiatic nations, too, have been considering, the support by the United States of the unscrupulous regime of Chiang Kai-shek. I do not know whether the influence of the United States has prevented, us in any way up to the present time from recognizing the government of China. I think we have been mistaken in postponing so long such recognition. I do not know whether the government even now

is prepared to recognize the Chinese government, ' and a pronouncement from our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is in my opinion long overdue.
While the revolution in China is communist-led, in my opinion it is not a communist revolution as such. A friend of mine who was in a position to follow closely and to judge what has happened returned recently from that country and he tells me that until a short time ago there were groups representing distinct divisions in Chinese governmental opinion and there was a possibility that one of those divisions might lead the government of China away from Stalinist affiliation. The picture from the democratic standpoint seems to have been darkened in recent days by the news that a comprehensive trade treaty has been signed by the Chinese with a group of iron curtain nations. I wonder if our tardiness in the recognition of the government of China has had anything to do with the opportunity which another great power has grasped to make a treaty of that sort. Perhaps once again it is a case of being too late. Perhaps we have played into the hands of Moscow.
My friends will tell me that I do not know anything about it. Admittedly, I do not know much about it, and I can only use such judgment as I have and apply it to the facts which I can ascertain. So far as this government is concerned, the matter of external affairs has not been one about which we have been taken into its confidence.
The white and western races of the world have been none too wise in their treatment of Asiatics. We have looked upon them consistently as being people to whom we could sell something or from whom we could extract cheap labour. Up to the present time we have not devoted our energies to sharing with them a better life. If we are honest with ourselves we must admit that never in our own minds have we granted to them the status of equality.
Now the western world is in a different position. The western world is now under the cool and critical scrutiny of the millions in the east. They have looked upon our support of the oppressor in China. They are considering our refusal to recognize that government. They know of the tardiness in making a permanent settlement with the great country of Japan. Many of the eastern races have won their fight against foreign domination and now they are at the crossroads and they have to decide which way they are to go. They have to decide what they are going to do with their new-found freedom.
The Address-Mr. Knight
India, Indo-China, Pakistan, Burma, Malaya: they are all looking on. They are studying democracy as we practise it. This democracy of ours is under the scrutiny of people who have never had an opportunity to practise it, who have never known its blessings and its satisfactions, and can judge it only by its effect. They want to know if it feeds the hungry. They want to know if it uplifts the downtrodden, if it cares for the sick, if it guarantees an equality of opportunity to its adherents. Let us hope that we have not been tried and found wanting, for it may be later than we think.
We have better weapons than the atom bomb with which to deal with people. We have better weapons than the hydrogen bomb with which to handle communism, which nearly always is the result of poverty, hunger, misery and social injustice. Perhaps even at this late date we can set out to win the friendship, respect and gratitude of the eastern people. Either we shall do that or we shall continue to drive them into the arms of Soviet Russia.
Asia looks at our attempts to solve the problem of surpluses of food and other material wealth, and our general acceptance up to now of the idea that the waste of war is necessary to do away with embarrassing surpluses. They can tell us how to put those surpluses to better use. How will they look upon the proposals being made in many quarters that the production of consumer goods, particularly of agricultural foodstuffs, shall be curtailed? How will they look upon proposals for the curtailment of production while their children, and perhaps some of ours, are starving for lack of the necessities of life?
I noted what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had to say the other day in his speech when he advocated the promotion of schemes within this country designed to increase that same consumer production. One of the things which he was advocating was irrigation. Irrigation will produce foodstuffs in great abundance, but the leader of the opposition did not suggest how any surpluses were to be got rid of in a world which is already beginning to be cluttered up with surpluses.
The dividing line between poverty and plenty always appears quite suddenly; there is no space between the extremes. We come through a period when we are all short of goods, and then suddenly, just like that, we have more goods than we know what to do with. They are there upon the shelves and the only solution to that particular problem we have evolved up to the present is to destroy as many of them as possible in the process of war, or to substitute for those
188	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knight unsalable consumer goods weapons which are destroyed but which absorb the human energy of the worker.
I take it that the leader of the opposition is not prepared to oiler a solution for the disposal of this increased production. It is an unfortunate fact that every country in the world, even those not so highly industrialized as our own, under, the queer economic set-up now extant wants to sell and on the other hand no one is willing to buy or has the money, or the right kind of money, with which to make purchases. Our own refusal to accept money or goods has forced Europe into the uneconomic production of grain and other foodstuffs. Every government in western Europe, and for all I know in eastern Europe as well, although it is difficult to obtain information from that source, at the moment is subsidizing its own farming industry. They are helping the farmers with free chemical fertilizers, with farm loans, with advice from the extension departments in their universities. This is being done for one particular purpose, so that the countries in question may become as nearly as possible self-sustaining in the matter of food supplies. These people have not forgotten the hunger of the last war; they have not forgotten the devastation that fell from the skies upon their fields, and they are not unaware of the threat of war that overshadows them now. All this forms the main impetus for the process which I have just described.
Thus it is that the production of grain, notably wheat, dairy products, eggs and meat is climbing steadily and the need for imports is decreasing proportionately. Some of those countries which will be self-sustaining before very long, and are almost self-sustaining now, are Denmark-notably Denmark-Belgium, France, Holland, Sweden and Eire and last but not least Britain herself. If you think of these countries you will remember that some of them have been the best markets for some of our own products. I am afraid that they will be so no longer. To whom shall we sell our goods? Nobody seems to know. The purchasing power of our own people is diminishing because of unemployment. The people of the United States normally produce surpluses of the very things which we produce ourselves. That nation, instead of becoming our purchasing customer, is becoming our rival in the sale of the things which we have available for export.
I take it that our United States friends are often misquoted, or perhaps the sensational journalism to which we have become accustomed quotes those sayings of public men in any country which are startling and dramatic. Thus I am in no position to judge whether or


not United States opinion is correctly reflected in the reported outbursts of some of its public men. Some of them seem to hold opinions which I hope the government leaders of our country do not share. The secretary of defence of the United States, Mr. Johnson, is reported to have stated on a recent occasion, in language more vigorous than judicious, that "we should' lick hell out of the Russians." Granting provocation, and I do grant provocation, I suggest that is a type of bravado in which one should not indulge. I do not want to lick hell out of the Russians and I do not want anyone to lick hell out of me. May I respectfully suggest that licking hell out of anybody is not the way to defeat communism. I suppose we licked hell out of Germany. I would ask you, sir, whether the fact that we licked hell out of Germany has decreased the number of communists in that country or has increased them.
What has been the over-all result of trying to lick communism by force in Germany or elsewhere in the world? What kind of people become communists?

I will tell you about that in a minute. My hon. Liberal friends from Saskatchewan can never forget that one thing which occupies their every moment asleep and awake. I should like to speak seriously for a moment if I may. What kind of people become communists? It is precisely the people who take a licking, whether that licking be spiritual, economic or physical. Communism is the result of poverty, social injustice, hunger and despair. You will see why I am discussing this in connection witih foreign affairs, and I am thinking now particularly of the eastern nations to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks. War produces those very conditions, does it not? It is to be hoped that the discovery five or six months ago that the Russians have atomic bombs in their possession, and that the general realization of the awfulness of the latest weapon of total extermination, the hydrogen bomb, will bring about a new approach to the matter of the international control of such weapons. When we find Einstein declaring, as he did in New York a week or two ago, that if the H-bomb is developed annihilation of any life on earth is within the range of technical possibility, then it is time to do some thinking and to act upon the thought.
The possession of the hydrogen bomb will give no security to the United States, Canada or anyone else. The United States people either have not now or will not long continue to have a monopoly of that particular weapon. Its creation is a menace to all the peoples of the earth, and efforts should be renewed to

have it and all weapons of that degree of frightfulness-you can include them all so far as I am concerned-outlawed by all nations by United Nations organization agreement.
Might I urge the Canadian government that it might well initiate, or support, if it has been initiated, a new approach or any approach to this problem which might have a chance of a successful conclusion. Inspection and control of weapons, within the machinery of the United Nations, would seem to be implicit in any agreement, and by a successful conclusion I mean one which would accomplish the aim of making it impossible for either side in this particular struggle to use such weapons as I have been discussing.
The other day a former United States secretary of state, James F. Byrnes, declared that socialism and communism are identical perils. Perhaps I will now answer indirectly the interjections of my hon. friends on my right but who are to the left of Mr. Speaker. Muddy thinking of that type as evidenced by the statement of Mr. Byrnes, the secretary of state, who declared that socialism and communism are identical perils, muddy thinking of that type on the part of North American leaders will ill serve them in their professed attempt to save western Europe from communism, a Europe in which there remains hardly a capitalist nation and only one fascist nation of any importance. The only political force active at this moment against communism between the iron curtain and the Atlantic coast of Spain is the socialism of the democratic socialist nations such as Belgium, Norway, Sweden and Great Britain. Such socialist nations stand on guard for democracy in the Europe of today. I doubt if there is a member in the house who can deny that. I mean an intelligent member who is prepared to face the issue and debate it intelligently.
The communism of Moscow has never practised democratic socialist principles and has suppressed them everywhere in the territory which it has overrun. There is a real danger that we are going to miss the boat again. There is a real danger that the people of the United States may be no better informed than is their former secretary of state, and they might consent to an isolation of themselves from these groups which up to the present have succeeded in retaining their freedom. Withdrawal of the support of the North American nations from these groups would be disastrous to the cause in which we are all involved.
Neither the United States government of the day, nor the Canadian government of the day, may agree with the political philosophy of the majority of the people in those
The Address-Mr. Knight countries, but what is the alternative to socialism in those countries? Do we desire that alternative? One of the best ways to bring about that alternative, is to belittle and neglect the friends and potential allies who are organized to oppose it. One thing that those countries need is hope. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said yesterday, and I use his words, most of all they need hope. They need friends even more than they need American dollars.
The existence of these misunderstandings, such as has been illustrated by the interjection of the hon. member and such as have been shown by the former United States secretary of state, might well provide a mission and a challenge for our own Secretary of State for External Affairs. The correction of these blunders, the interpretation of the ideas of various people to men of different political philosophies, but united by a passionate desire for political freedom, might well present a challenge to him.
The other day I read that a slogan had been adopted by a group of Republicans in the United States. It was this, "Liberty versus socialism". It is the same kind of thing that one might hear from my hon. friend. It is the same kind of thing you might see in an election pamphlet, but that you would not take very seriously.
Where is Britain today? Where is the Britain who has proven on many blood-soaked battlefields her love of liberty and the willingness of her sons to die for it? In the aftermath of the last holocaust, Britain adopted democratic socialism as the only method of preserving the liberty of her people. I fancy she is doing it again tonight, as her election returns come in. Irrespective of the result of the election which took place today, I say that by so doing she was able to accomplish that object at that time, and since then has advanced some distance at least along the path of freedom, social, political and economic.
It has been the great genius of the British people that they were able to reconcile that love of liberty, that love of freedom, with the attainment of social and material benefit over the last five years. That these advances are of a permanent nature is generally conceded; indeed, that fact is admitted by all, even by those who would form a government in England alternative to the present one. At the moment, the likelihood of that alternate government being formed is not very great. I say that even if there had been a Conservative government elected in England today, that government would not

The Address-Mr. Quelch dare to ask England, in her present mood, to take onfe retrograde step upon the path of progress which she has been pursuing.
