speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised and disappointed when the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) yesterday stated that it was not his intention to set up a special committee on veterans' affairs at this session. During the past fifteen years that I have been in this house, it has always been the custom to set up that committee during the first session of each new parliament. That was the case in 1936, 194041 and 1945-46. I believe there will be a good deal of resentment amongst the veterans when they hear that this committee is not to be set up. They were taking it for granted that the committee would be set up at this session to deal with a number of their problems. They will wonder why the government should now consider their problems of less importance than they have been considered in the past.
I believe that anyone reading the speech from the throne, and the speeches of a number of Liberal members who have spoken in the house this session, might easily come to the conclusion that the blame for the loss of Canadian markets in Europe rests outside Canada. I would say that anyone who will face this situation with an unbiased mind must admit that a large share of the blame rests squarely on the shoulders of the Canadian government. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) yesterday blame the loss of markets upon the devaluation of sterling by Britain. I do not want to be charged with misrepresenting what he said, so I shall quote his words, which are to be found on page 146 of Hansard:
As hon. members know, the markets were lost in England to a certain extent not by the action of this government but by the action of the British government itself, and by an action which Sir Stafford Cripps on many occasions said he would not take; I refer to the devaluing of the pound. That is why the markets were lost. There is no question about that. Why then try to pass the buck to the government?
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is a very large question, because that is not a statement of fact. If the hon. member will read a speech that was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) before the Canadian chamber of commerce in London, England, in 1948, he will find that the Minister of Agriculture was complaining over the fact that our contracts were being cut down; we were losing markets. That was nine months
(Mr. Knight.]

before devaluation, so it cannot be charged that devaluation had anything to do with that.
Neither can it be charged that Sir Stafford Cripps voluntarily brought about devaluation. Time and again he had stated he did not intend to bring about devaluation, but what happened? For over a year in the United States, and to a lesser extent in Canada, and by the international monetary fund, a strong campaign of propaganda was carried on to make people believe that devaluation was inevitable. People were told that the only way Britain could expand her exports to the dollar areas was by reducing the price of her goods. It was stated that the price of British goods was so high they could not get into the United States market and, therefore, Britain would have to devalue the pound. After some time people believed that the 'thing was inevitable, that devaluation was bound to come about. Consequently, many of the great importing firms deferred their purchases from Britain waiting for the day when this devaluation would come about. That, of course, accentuated the dollar shortage and created a crisis in Britain which finally forced devaluation. By no stretch of the imagination, therefore, can it be charged that the loss of markets is due to Great Britain's action in devaluing sterling.
During the last session of parliament the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) charged that many of us on this side of the house who were asking for a more realistic approach to international trade problems were adopting a pessimistic attitude. He said we were confusing realism with pessimism. I believe that the past few months have shown that our fears were well founded, and that the minister was either indulging in wishful thinking or living in a fool's paradise.
If that is not evident to the minister or to the government, I may say that it is quite evident to the farm organizations and to the farmers who, as a result of the loss of markets, are facing quite a drastic reduction in income. Today, with unemployment figures climbing and the income of agriculture being reduced as a result of the loss of markets, discontent and fear is spreading throughout the country; that fear is with regard to what is going to happen in the future. I would say that the speeches that have recently been made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. McCubbin) and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mutch) have not helped to create confidence; they have merely added insult to injury.

With the world becoming divided into two armed camps we cannot afford to allow fear and discontent to undermine the morale of the people in the western camp, as a result of poverty expanding in the face of potential plenty. The situation would be different if there were an actual lack of resources in the world to provide for its needs. But today we are faced with this situation. Certain countries are talking about cutting down their production because of the lack of markets while at the same time people of many countries are facing starvation. It seems to me that the tragedy of this whole question is that back in the years 1944 and 1945 it was crystal clear that the international financial policies that this government were supporting were bound to lead to the present situation of a so-called dollar crisis. Plenty of warnings were sounded, by various organizations in this country and others, as to what would happen if we continued to follow that road. Certainly this group in this house in 1945 did everything in their power to convince the government that, if they followed out the policies they were sponsoring at that time, the inevitable result would be a falling off in production as a result of the loss of foreign markets.
At the end of the war we were faced with two main problems. First of all, there was the need to bring about the reconversion of wartime industries to peacetime production and also the need of rehabilitation of the devastated areas. In the second place, there was the need to provide for the distribution of the production of nations, once reconversion and rehabilitation had taken place. I think everybody would agree that, as to the first problem, we have made good progress. Production in this country is up to a high level, and even in Europe I understand that production is about 20 per cent higher than it was prior to the war. But we have not made any progress whatsoever in solving the other problem, that of getting surplus production to people who need it. It is exactly the same problem we faced between the two wars, during the hungry thirties. We failed to solve the problem at that time, and we had to wait until the war came along, when large markets were created, to be able to get out of that situation. But today our problem is far greater than it was in the years between the two wars, because our powers of production today have greatly increased.
I do not want to labour this point, but just let me remind the house of the post-war financial program that was not only supported but actually sponsored by this government. In 1944 certain international
The Address-Mr. Quelch financial proposals for financing the post-war period were presented before the reconstruction committee of this house. In 1945 the Bretton Woods agreement was placed before this house, that is the proposal to set up the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction and development. Since that time I have heard many people state that it was not the purpose of these institutions to provide for the entire financial needs of international trade in the post-war period but that they were set up only to provide a breathing spell. It is interesting to note what John W. Snyder, secretary of the treasury of the United States and chairman of the board of governors of the international bank for reconstruction and development, stated at the first session in 1946. His words were as follows:
The fund and bank were designed to meet both the immediate post-war and the longer-term monetary and financial needs of the world.
That was the purpose as stated by Mr. Snyder. I think that everybody would admit today that those two institutions have failed to provide, for the monetary needs of the world; not only have they failed, but they have failed miserably.
In 1945 we criticized the international monetary fund on the ground that it had a definite 'pro-creditor bias. It was supposed to provide for the stabilization and the balancing of trade in the world, but it placed on the debtor nation the full responsibility for bringing about that balance of trade and placed absolutely no responsibility or obligation upon the creditor nation to play its part. It is true that a debtor nation that is unable to meet its payments can obtain foreign exchange from the international monetary fund in exchange for its own currency. But if that nation is unable to redeem its currency that is held by the fund in excess of its quota, that country is obliged to pay an expanding rate of interest. The rate of interest increases every year until it reaches the figure of 5 per cent. Once the rate of interest reaches 5 per cent, the international monetary fund is permitted to charge that country any rate of interest it likes.
I wonder how any member in this house would like to sign an agreement whereby he guarantees to pay any rate of interest his creditor names in the future, if he is not able to meet his commitments. I do not think any member of this house would be prepared to sign an agreement of that kind. Many nations in the soft currency area were not anxious to sign it, but they were forced to do so, as the Bretton Woods agreement was made the price of help given to them by the

The Address-Mr. Quelch United States of America. There would not be the same danger involved in a nation's incurring a debt to the fund if some obligation was placed upon the creditor nation to buy goods from the importing nation. The importing nation would then be able to secure the foreign exchange necessary to redeem the holdings of its currency held by the fund. But in view of the fact that no obligation is placed on the creditor nation to buy goods from the importing nation, the debtor nation is therefore in an uncertain and unfortunate position.
We therefore repeatedly warned that the implementation of the Bretton Woods agreement would breed a program of self-sufficiency within the soft-currency countries; and of course that is exactly what is happening today. In an endeavour to balance their trade, the soft-currency countries are steadily curtailing their imports from the dollar area. They have no other alternative. We today urge, as we have consistently urged in the past, that we recognize that the true purpose of international trade is the exchange of goods and services as between nations on a basis of mutual advantage. Therefore, since the only currency required to buy the exports of the sterling area is sterling, we should accept that in payment of our exports.
We have also advocated the setting up of an international clearing house, upon which credits held in one country could be exchanged for credits in another. It is interesting to note that today there are many organizations now advocating a somewhat similar procedure. The London chamber of commerce of England, probably one of the oldest institutions of its kind, an organization that has had more experience in international trade probably than any other organization in the world, have for long advocated such a procedure. Now we find that farm organizations in Canada, in the United States, and in other countries are advocating a somewhat similar procedure. The international federation of agriculture producers and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the commodity experts of FAO are now advocating the setting up of an international commodity clearing house, which in many respects is similar to the international exchange which we have been advocating in the past.
In his speech the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the sterling situation. I want to quote his remarks, which are found at page 135 of Hansard:
We have always contended, however, that the sterling area as we know it today should be regarded as a transitional stage on the way to a trading system where currencies will be convertible and where exchange controls and quantitative restrictions will be drastically reduced.


I would say that the achievement of that goal can only be brought about by the dollar area being willing to accept exports from the sterling area in payment for their exports. I would say that that is the only long-term solution. True, the United States of America and Canada can make foreign investments in soft-currency countries but that would be a short-term solution. I say it cannot be regarded as a long-term solution, because finally we shall have to accept exports from the sterling area to pay the interest on our investments in addition to their exports in payment for our exports. Therefore on the long-term basis it merely aggravates the situation because we would then have to accept an unfavourable balance of trade in order to make it possible for the sterling area to balance their payments.
I was very much interested in the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), because I think he dealt with this thing in a very straightforward and frank way when referring to the question of the convertibility of currency. I quote his statement, which is to be found on page 51 of Hansard:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) talked today about the reasonableness of making currency convertible. The difficulty is not with respect to the converting of currency, but is rather with respect to the exchange of goods. Trade is not the passing of pieces of paper from one person to another. Trade resolves itself into the exchange of commodities; and the difficulties about the nonconvertibility of exchange arise from the fact that there have not been commodities which could be delivered to us in exchange for our commodities exported to the United Kingdom.
I agree entirely with the first part of the statement. Of course the second part is not entirely correct in so far as the present situation is concerned. It was true in regard to the situation immediately after the war; but it is not correct today to say the reason that Britain has an unfavourable balance of trade is that she has not got goods to export to us. There are many goods that Britain is able to export to us, but we are not prepared to accept them. Furthermore, let me point out that it' has not always been the policy of this government to accept exports from Britain in payment for our exports. Our policy in the past has been to insist that Britain pay for our exports in dollars. In order that there be no doubt about that let me quote from a debate that took place back in 1946 when Mr. Ilsley was Minister of Finance. At that time we were discussing our loan to Britain. At page 764 of Hansard of that year Mr. Ilsley said:
We must be able to use the proceeds of our exports to the United Kingdom and the continent of Europe in paying our own bills and debts in the United States.

In other words, we must be permitted to demand payment for our exports to Britain in dollars in order that we may pass these dollars on to the United States to make up our deficit. Then I asked Mr. Ilsley this question, which may be found at page 919 of Hansard:
Will Canada be prepared to accept goods from the United Kingdom in payment of loans? How will the United Kingdom maintain convertibility of the pound if Canada and the United States do not provide the United Kingdom with dollars by purchasing British goods to the extent of the British credit?
I had pointed out that in view of the fact that we were making loans to Britain then, in the future not only would Britain have to export to us goods to pay for our exports, but, in addition, would have to export to us goods to pay interest; so the net result would be that we would have to be willing to accept an unfavourable balance of trade in the future. Mr. Ilsley replied:
It is not necessary that there should be adverse balance of payments between Canada and the United Kingdom in order to enable the United Kingdom to repay the loan. She can pay for Canadian goods by exports to other countries as well as to Canada. Under a multilateral trading system and convertible currencies-
I would like to hear Mr. Ilsley's opinion on that statement today. It is true that prior to the last war Britain had large-scale foreign investments in other countries. She received interest on some of those investments in the form of dollars. She was able to transfer those dollars to her creditors in the dollar area. That is not the situation today. Many of those nations in which she had large investments prior to the war are today Britain's creditors, for instance, India, Pakistan, Egypt. I noticed from a debate in the House of Commons in England that today 40 per cent of the exports from Britain go to pay debts incurred during the last war.
The minister says that she can sell goods for dollars to other nations. What nations? In view of the fact that the United States of America has a favourable balance of trade with the sterling area of over $6 billion, it must mean that there is a deficit of around $6 billion as between the sterling area and the dollar countries. Certainly, Britain will not be able to get a surplus of dollars by exporting goods to the United States of America, and therefore naturally in the final analysis if we want to get paid by Britain on account of her indebtedness to us, and if we want Britain to buy goods from us, then we must be prepared to provide her with dollars by buying her exports. There is no other alternative, because Britain is apparently making it quite clear to the world today that she is not prepared to continue to go into unrepayable debt. Therefore I would say
The Address-Mr. Quelch that the policy that we have insisted in pursuing is very largely responsible for our loss of markets today.
I want to deal specifically with the question of markets for farm products. We hear a lot of talk about surpluses; we hear a lot of talk about lack of markets; and we are starting to hear talk about the need to curtail production, owing to the fact that markets are shrinking. But when we hear that kind of talk we should also recall what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) told us yesterday concerning the tremendous degree of poverty in many parts of Asia, where people are suffering from a very low standard of living, and are desirous of obtaining goods from other countries.
Also the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking before the FAO, referred to the need for expanding production to meet the needs of the world. A quotation from his speech as it appears in Foreign Trade is as follows:
Although agricultural production throughout the world has regained pre-war levels, it has not kept up with the increasing population of the world. Supplies available on a per capita basis are therefore still below pre-war levels.
He also went on to say that:
Monetary difficulties are threatening to prevent freedom of movement of foods and other necessary products from "surplus" to "deficit" areas. This might lead to a slackening of the productive effort in some countries and an increase in costs which might deny food to the people of other countries.
He goes on:
Our monetary difficulties today threaten to reproduce the situation which existed twenty years ago, a lack of that free movement of food from those with food to spare to those in want.
And he continued:
Unless some way can be found of solving this problem, we cannot hope for that "all-out" effort by exporting countries that is needed, if the people of the whole world are to be adequately fed.
Therefore I think all members will agree that, that being the situation, it would be an act of criminal folly on the part of any government to reduce production at a time when that production is so direly needed in other parts of the world.
The Minister of Agriculture has frankly admitted that this is a monetary problem. I think that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the International Federation of Agricultural Producers are to be warmly commended for the research work they have done in connection with this question, and the proposals that they have put forward for a commodity clearing house.
I attended the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held at

The Address-Mr. Quelch
Niagara Falls last month, and was greatly struck by the unanimity reached by the delegates from both east and west in Canada on all problems coming before the convention. That has not always been the case. I think it augurs well today, when great problems are arising, to see that eastern and western farmers are able to work together in complete accord.
At that convention a speech was delivered by Professor J. K. Galbraith, professor of economics at Harvard university. He delivered a most thought-provoking speech on the subject of international trade and foreign markets. May I quote briefly from one part of his speech which struck me as being of special interest. He said:
It is still our common faith that somehow we are going to work out of the present unbalance in international trade. To that 1 subscribe. It is our common illusion, however, unconscious but real, that in doing so we shall re-establish the flow of agricultural products, of food and foodstuffs, from this continent to Europe, through the ordinary channels of trade. That I doubt. Anyone who honestly examines the trend must reach an exactly opposite conclusion.
And then he goes on:
First we must abandon the notion that 1952 is the day of decision to balancing the trade accounts. So long as it remains so, we must expect that the balance will be achieved largely at the expense of our agricultural exports. Western European countries need to be given assurance that we in this hemisphere will reciprocate their efforts with assistance. This does not necessarily mean a continuation of the Marshall plan in its present form or with some skilfully contrived pseudonym. It does mean an assurance that western Europe can purchase food and fibre from this hemisphere beyond 1952 and that help in doing so will be forthcoming if necessary. It was partly such an assurance that the proposed International Commodity Clearing House of the FAO was designed to offer.
I think it was a great tragedy that the conference of FAO turned down the proposal for the setting up of an international commodity clearing house. I wish to analyse briefly the reasons given by the conference for turning these proposals down. First of all, however, I should like to give a brief summary of the functions of this international commodity clearing house.
In June 1949 the International Federation of Agricultural Producers presented their proposals for the stabilization of prices and the distribution of surpluses of agricultural products to the council of FAO. These proposals embodied the idea of an international commodity clearing house. Then the director of FAO appointed a committee of six commodity experts to prepare a report on commodity problems for the FAO conference to be held in November of 1949. These experts proposed the setting up of an international
	.

commodity clearing house, and this was supported by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the International Federation of Agricultural Producers, and farm organizations throughout the United States. However, as I said, the FAO conference turned the proposal down.
Before discussing the reasons why this proposal was turned down I should like briefly to summarize the functions of this institution. I have made the summary from the IFAP Bulletin of October, 1949.
Functions of ICCH would include the following:
1.	Subject to provisions outlined below the purchase of stocks of commodities that are in surplus in the country in which those stocks appear.
2.	The negotiation of sales in inconvertible currencies in order to assist in maintaining the flow of trade during periods of exchange disequilibrium; such payments being guaranteed by the buying countries against losses from exchange depreciation.
3.	The negotiation of sales at special prices below the market to countries in need, under strictly defined conditions of use, for example, for relief purposes, special nutritional programs, or for development projects.
4.	As a long run function, the holding of stocks acquired in periods of surplus as reserves to protect the interests of consumers in periods of shortage.
5. The negotiation of bilateral or multilateral trading agreements, or exchanges of commodities on a barter basis.
6.	The co-ordination of the negotiating and administration of international commodity agreements and arrangements pending final disposition of these functions by the economic and social council after the charter of ITO has entered into force.
7.	The organization of consultations between governments and other institutions in respect of commodity policies, agreement^ and transactions, and in respect of the readjustment of the uses of land and other national resources in order to implement such policies, agreements and transactions, and to meet the changing structure of world demand and world supply.
It is clear from the report that the committee considers the long range functions of ICCH should be left to later experience but in the short run ICCH would use mainly two methods for constructive disposal of surpluses. Using wheat as an example ICCH would operate in the following ways:
(1)	The exporting country would sell surplus wheat to ICCH at full market price and the purchases would be financed by the exporter contributing the value of the wheat to ICCH as additional capital. ICCH would then sell quantities of wheat to the importing country in addition to and not as a substitute for its usual purchases. ICCH would take in payment the currency of the importing country, even if it were, at the time, inconvertible. The importing country would guarantee against loss by currency devaluation. ICCH would hold this currency to the credit of the exporting country until enlarged trade or restored currency convertibility permitted clearing the account.
(2)	The exporter would sell surplus wheat to ICCH at a reduced price if the payment were in an immediately acceptable (presumably convertible) currency and provided that the quantity of wheat went to some special use in addition to regular consumption by the importing country. Such transactions would be financed from the revolving fund of ICCH, established by the initially paid-in twenty per cent of capital, but would not normally involve any loss to ICCH.

The reasons given by the FAO conference for turning down those proposals are, to say the least, somewhat peculiar. I should like to summarize a few of them. In rejecting the short-term trading functions of the ICCH, the conference observed that the accumulation of inconvertible currency would represent additional indebtedness by the deficit countries involving the burden of eventual repayment in terms of additional exports of goods and services and would have the effect of delaying the general convertibility.
I would say that anyone reading that statement would be justified in doubting the sincerity of the people who wrote that paragraph. What is the purpose of these proposals? The purpose is to get surplus goods to the people who need them. Yet we are told here that this might delay convertibility and therefore the proposal should be turned down. I think it is quite obvious that that body confused the means with the end and the shadow with the substance.
We are often told that convertibility will facilitate the expansion of trade, but here we have a situation where surpluses are accumulating and a proposal is made whereby they can be got to people who need them but it is said that that might delay convertibility. X am satisfied that the people of the world are more interested in getting surplus goods to people who need them than they are in restoring convertibility. If we do not take steps by which these surplus goods can be got to the people who need them, what happens? Production will be reduced and we will not then have the goods available to meet the needs of the people. That, mind you, is suggested in the name of convertibility.
The next reason for rejecting the proposals was this:
The expenditure of such accumulations on purchases in the soft-currency areas would, in the main, be for the purchase of commodities which would ordinarily earn hard currency.
The ICCH only proposes to sell goods that would not be sold through the ordinary channels of trade and therefore there could be no fear of the ICCH proposals interfering with the ordinary channels of trade. Goods going through the ordinary channels of trade as a result of the exchange of goods would continue to move in that way, but to the extent the exporting nation was not able to dispose of its exports the international commodity clearing house would provide a means by which those goods could be got to the people who needed them.
Then the conference suggested that the financial functions proposed for the ICCH could be performed by the governments directly involved. I was very much interested
The Address-Mr. Quelch in the stand taken by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Here is a proposal by which we can get our surplus products to the country that needs them and the Minister of Agriculture says, We do not need that, we can do it ourselves. The government has now stated that they can get surplus goods to other nations, so there will be absolutely no excuse in the future for this government saying they are not able to sell our surplus production. They have turned down a suggestion that would have made it possible on the ground that they can do it without that suggestion. The farmers will be waiting to see the government take action in the immediate future to dispose of our surplus products. I hope we will not have any more talk about not being able to export our goods to other countries.
Then the conference decided to establish an FAO committee on commodity problems which would work under the supervision of and be responsible to the council. I do not think that that committee is going to be very enthusiastic. The committee of six experts drafted the ICCH proposals which were turned down because it was claimed they would interfere with the normal methods of financing international trade. All this committee will be able to do is to make proposals that will not interfere in any way with the recognized methods of financing international trade.
I think the most interesting statement made by the conference was in connection with financial facilities, and I quote:
The conference called attention to the fact that although existing national economic development plans required international funds far in excess of those currently available, international financial institutions have not received a sufficient number of well-documented loan applications. The conference instructed the director-general of FAO to strengthen co-operation with the international bank for reconstruction and the international monetary fund and to propose specific arrangements with those organizations.
I think you have there the real reason why the conference turned down the proposal of the ICCH. It is quite evident that representatives of the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction and development were at that conference and advised against the adoption of this proposal. Not only have the international monetary fund and the international bank for reconstruction failed, and failed miserably, to devise methods by which our international trade can be financed; but they are now blocking other measures that might take their place.
I noticed that when the Minister of Agriculture was speaking with reference to the Agricultural Prices Support Act he stated

The Address-Mr. Quelch that that act was no alternative to markets. I think everybody will agree with that and I think the farmers realize that only too well. But the farmers will remember also that the Minister of Agriculture has turned down a proposal which would have made it possible to export our surplus commodities to other countries on the ground that the government can do what this international commodity clearing house would do. The farmers will feel that the obtaining , of markets is a responsibility of the federal government and the Minister of Agriculture need not make any excuse in the future that the federal government is not able to dispose of farm surpluses. I was interested in a report appearing in the press as to a statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The heading of the article is:
Gardiner charges some people making food distribution difficult.
The article reads:
He said some people are making it difficult to move these surpluses to the areas where they can be consumed.
Then the press dispatch goes on:
Mr. Gardiner did not identify these persons. However, it appeared to be a reference to the Canadian proposal for establishment of an international commodity clearing house, turned down by the United Nations food and agricultural organization.
Obviously the press statement is wrong because Mr. Gardiner was one of those who opposed an international commodity clearing house. I think the house has the right to expect the Minister of Agriculture to tell it who these individuals are who are making it hard for Canada to dispose of its surplus products to nations that need them. I have a pretty good idea who they may be because I recall that, when he spoke before the
Canadian chamber of commerce in London in December, 1948, he blamed our troubles on a bunch of what he called financial crackpots who call themselves economists. He still did not name them but we know very well who the men are who control our international financial policy. They are largely the men who control the international monetary fund, the international bank for reconstruction, institutions for which Mr. Gardiner himself voted in 1945.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. When people ask who is to blame for Canada not being able to dispose of her agricultural products, let us place that blame where it fairly belongs, fairly and squarely upon the shoulders of this government, because up to the present time they have insisted upon policies which make it impossible for the sterling area to buy from us, by insisting that they must pay us in dollars instead of our being willing to accept payment in goods.
